Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Agricultural Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Vignette:
Kofi has worked the same stretch of land for fifteen years, but he has never grown accustomed to the quiet. At forty-five, he still finds himself scanning the edges of the vast, open fields, his body tensing at the snap of a branch or the distant rumble of a truck on the gravel road. He tells himself he is just being careful, but he knows it is more than that. It is a watchfulness that never rests, a deep and abiding conviction that danger is always just out of sight. This feeling, a low hum of dread beneath the surface of his days, has been his companion for as long as he can remember. It is a relic of a childhood home where safety was a myth, a place where the creak of a floorboard after dark meant his father was awake and the night was about to be filled with shouting and the sound of his mother’s weeping.

The memories come back not as a coherent story, but in fragments of sensory detail. The sour smell of beer on his father's breath, the precise pattern of the floral wallpaper he would stare at from his bed, the sickening thud of a body hitting the wall in the next room. He was seven years old, small and powerless, hidden under his thin blanket. He remembers the overwhelming urge to run, to scream, to do *something*, but his limbs felt like lead. He did nothing. He just lay there, listening, praying for it to stop. That inaction has haunted him for nearly four decades. It has calcified into a bitter self-recrimination that no amount of adult logic can dislodge. He is certain he will never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened, for being the boy who hid instead of the son who protected.

This profound sense of failure has hollowed out his life. He looks at photos from his twenties and barely recognizes the smiling young man. He used to be a happy person, he thinks, but now he feels he is always miserable, the capacity for joy having been extinguished long ago. His faith, too, has evaporated—not just in a higher power, but in the basic goodness of people. He sees the potential for violence everywhere, a darkness lurking behind every friendly face. This is why he cannot believe his partner, Amara, when she tells him he is safe. Her words are kind, but they are just sounds. They cannot penetrate the certainty, born in that small bedroom, that safety is an illusion and that those who are supposed to protect you are often the most dangerous.

Over the years, Kofi has developed a rigid set of rules to manage the constant threat. He tries hard not to think about the past, building a mental wall that he reinforces daily. But the thoughts are persistent. When they break through, they are often consumed with fantasies of revenge. He spends hours while driving the tractor imagining a confrontation with his father, now a frail old man. In these daydreams, Kofi is strong and fearless, saying all the things he never could, physically stopping the man who terrorized his family. The scenarios provide a fleeting sense of power, but they always dissolve into the same familiar shame. His most entrenched rule is to never, ever be alone with another person. At work, he orchestrates his tasks to ensure he is always part of a team, even if it means seeming inefficient. Last month, his supervisor asked him to repair an irrigation line at the far end of the property by himself; Kofi claimed the parts were too heavy and waited two hours until a co-worker could join him, earning a frustrated sigh from his boss.

At home, this need for a constant witness has begun to suffocate Amara. He follows her from room to room, unable to settle if she is not in his line of sight. The nights are the worst. As darkness falls, his vigilance ratchets up to an unbearable pitch. Every shadow becomes a threat, every sound from outside a potential intruder. He cannot relax, cannot sleep until he is sure she is asleep beside him, a human shield against the terrors the night holds. It was after one such night, when she found him sitting ramrod straight in a chair at 3 a.m., staring at the locked front door, that she finally told him she couldn’t live like this anymore. It was her tearful plea that brought him to therapy. He is terrified of dredging up the past he has worked so hard to suppress, but the thought of losing the one person who makes him feel even a sliver of safety is infinitely worse. He has come to believe he has lost himself to the past, and he is desperate, for the first time, to find a way back.
